title: Ceramic vs Steel Skate Bearings: Which Power Bearings Should You Buy?
thumbnail_text: Ceramic or steel bearings? Which one to buy

scenes.heading: Ceramic vs Steel Skate Bearings
scenes.sub: Which one to buy, and how to keep it fast
scenes.chapter: Ceramic or steel: the short answer
scenes.narration: If you are choosing between ceramic and steel skate bearings, you will know which one to buy by the end of this. Here is the short answer first. If you race seriously, ceramic earns its price. It spins up faster, runs cooler and holds its speed deeper into a long effort. If you train most days, or you want the most speed for your money, a precision steel set is the better buy. It also leaves you budget for wheels. For most skaters, that is the whole answer. The rest explains why, what ceramic really means on the box, how much speed is on the table, and how to keep any set fast.

scenes.heading: Why bearings matter
bullets: Every push travels through your bearings
Eight per skate, sixteen per pair
Lower friction means more roll per stride
Build quality and care decide speed
scenes.narration: Every push you make has to travel through your bearings before it reaches the ground. Lower friction means more roll for each stride. It means less energy wasted as heat. And it means a bearing that stays fast deeper into a long race. A single four wheel skate holds eight bearings. A pair holds sixteen. Every one of them is turning for as long as you are rolling. How they perform comes down to two things only. How the bearing was built, and how well you look after it. You control the second one completely. Keep that in mind, because it comes back at the end.

scenes.heading: The five parts of a bearing
scenes.narration: Here is a bearing in cross section. The outer blue ring is the outer race. The grey ring near the middle is the inner race, around the eight millimetre bore. Between them, seven balls roll. The green dashed line is the cage, which keeps those balls evenly spaced. A well made cage positions each ball accurately, which cuts friction and extends life. The orange line is the seal. It keeps dirt and water away from the polished surfaces that let the bearing spin freely. The quality of each of these parts, and how precisely they are made and finished, is what separates a fast bearing from a cheap one.

scenes.heading: Check your size first
bullets: 608 size: 8 by 22 by 7 mm
Fits almost every inline speed wheel
Many quad hubs use 627 instead
608 and 627 are not interchangeable
scenes.narration: Before you think about materials, check your size. Almost every inline speed wheel takes the 608 bearing. That is eight millimetres on the bore, twenty two millimetres on the outside, and seven millimetres wide. Quad skaters are the exception. Many quad hubs use the smaller 627 bore instead. The two are not interchangeable, so confirm which one your wheels take before you order. A standard pair of four wheel inline skates needs sixteen bearings, two in each wheel. Ordering the wrong bore is the most expensive mistake you can make here, and the easiest one to avoid.

scenes.heading: Where each one wins
scenes.narration: Now the big question. Ceramic balls are lighter and harder than steel balls. Because they are lighter, they spin up faster and carry less inertia. Because they are harder and smoother, they run cooler and last longer. You can see that in the chart. The blue ceramic bars lead on spin up speed, on staying cool under load, and on durability. But look at the last row. On value for money, the grey steel bar is clearly longer. Good steel bearings still roll beautifully and cost less. The bars are indicative, not measured. The point is that neither choice is wrong. The right one depends on how much you race.

scenes.heading: Hybrid versus full ceramic
scenes.narration: Here is the part almost nobody explains before you spend the money. When a skate bearing is sold as ceramic, it nearly always means hybrid ceramic. That is the bearing on the left, with ceramic balls running in steel races. The one on the right is full ceramic, with ceramic races as well. That is a different thing, and it is not what skate shops sell. This matters in two ways. First, the steel races can still rust if you put your skates away wet. Ceramic does not make a bearing rust proof. Second, the bearing still needs light oil, because the races and the cage still need lubrication. A ceramic bearing run dry is just an expensive slow bearing.

scenes.heading: Silicon nitride and zirconia
bullets: Silicon nitride (Si3N4): hard, light, smooth
Chosen for elite speed
Zirconia (ZrO2): tougher, a little less speed
A more forgiving first ceramic
scenes.narration: You will see two ceramic materials in skate bearings. The first is silicon nitride. It is prized for elite speed, because it is extremely hard, light and smooth. The second is zirconia. It trades a little outright speed for toughness, which makes it the more forgiving way into ceramic. In the LiveLica range, the Swiss Ceramic uses silicon nitride and the Gold Ceramic uses zirconia. Both still sit in steel races. So everything you just heard about oil and dry storage applies to both of them.

scenes.heading: How much speed does ceramic buy?
bullets: Maker's figure: 0.8 to 1.0 W per bearing
Roughly 13 to 16 W across a pair
Real over a marathon, small over 500 m
Lighter balls help most off the line
scenes.narration: Less than the marketing implies, and more than the sceptics claim. The maker of one top ceramic set states a saving of zero point eight to one watt per bearing, against a typical precision steel bearing. Across the sixteen bearings in a pair, that is roughly thirteen to sixteen watts, on the manufacturer's own figures. That is a real number over a marathon. It is a much smaller one over a five hundred metre sprint. Read it in context. Those figures come from controlled conditions, not a dusty Indian road. Lower rotating weight is the part most skaters actually notice, and they notice it most in the first few strides off the line.

scenes.heading: Ball count and ABEC ratings
bullets: Most bearings use seven balls
Six balls: fewer contact points, freer roll
ABEC rates tolerance, not speed
Material, cage and oil matter more
scenes.narration: Two more numbers come up when you shop. The first is ball count. Most bearings use seven balls. Some use six. Fewer balls means fewer points of contact, which reduces friction and can raise top end speed. Slightly larger balls keep strength and life high. It suits experienced racers with a clean stride. The second is the ABEC rating. ABEC is a rating of manufacturing tolerance, not speed. A higher number means tighter precision, which is useful. But it says nothing about ball material, cage design or lubrication. Those have a bigger effect on how a bearing feels under your feet. Treat ABEC as one clue, not the whole story.

scenes.heading: Which one should you buy?
bullets: Training most days: precision steel
Racing for every advantage: ceramic
New to ceramic: start with zirconia
Beginner: steel, spend the rest on wheels
scenes.narration: So how do you choose? If you train most days and want the best value, start with a high quality steel set. If you race and want every advantage, move up to ceramic. If you are new to ceramic, zirconia is the softest landing. If you are a beginner, steel is usually the smarter spend. Until your technique and fitness are what hold you back, good steel gives you most of the feel for a fraction of the outlay. Spend the money you save on wheels or coaching. Move to ceramic when your kit becomes the limit, not your legs.

scenes.heading: The free speed most skaters ignore
bullets: Wipe bearings down and keep them dry
Re oil when the spin turns noisy
Clean after wet or dirty sessions
Never store skates wet
scenes.narration: Now the free speed most skaters ignore. Clean, well oiled bearings roll faster and last far longer than neglected ones. A bearing that has gone gritty and dry gives speed back faster than any upgrade can buy it. Dirt and water are the enemies of a fast spin. Wipe your bearings down, keep them dry, and re oil them regularly. Re oil whenever the spin starts to feel slow or noisy, and always after skating in wet or dirty conditions. A light, regular routine beats an occasional heavy clean. And never put your skates away wet. That is the mistake that quietly ruins a ceramic set, because the races are steel whatever the balls are made of.

scenes.heading: Clean bearings beat expensive bearings
scenes.sub: Full guide at livelica.com, link in the description
scenes.narration: So here is the one idea to remember. Buy steel and clean it, and you will be quick. Buy ceramic and still clean it, and you will be quicker. Skip the cleaning either way, and you have wasted the money. If your bearings feel gritty right now, cleaning them will do more for your lap times than anything you can buy. The full guide, with a comparison of four bearing sets and answers to common questions, is on the LiveLica blog. The link is in the description.
